opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that the objective has to be something you can actually feel progress on. At a big company, a group's goal can be quite abstract, like "advance the frontier in X," because there's a lot of slack. At a startup you don't have that luxury. If a goal can't tell you, week to week, whether you're getting closer or not, it isn't really a goal. It's a vibe.

So I usually ask: what is the one capability or result that, if we had it, would really change what the company can do? Then I work backward. What's the cleanest way to measure it? What's the smallest version we could show in a month or two? The objective should be ambitious enough that people are excited, but concrete enough that a new person on the team immediately knows what "good" looks like.

The second thing is that the objective should match the stage you're at. Early on, it's tempting to set goals that look like a research lab's, publishing or beating some benchmark. A benchmark is only useful if it's a faithful proxy for the thing you actually care about. A lot of the work is choosing, or even building, the right evaluation. Once you have a good eval, the team almost organizes itself around it, because everyone can see the same signal.

The third thing is honesty about trade-offs. A group objective means saying no to things. If the goal is, say, making the model reliably good at a certain kind of long-horizon task, then a lot of other interesting directions are explicitly not our job right now. I think saying that out loud matters. Otherwise smart people spread themselves thin, and each individual project looks reasonable, but the group doesn't move.

Finally, I try to keep the objective revisable. At a startup the world changes very fast. A new model comes out, or you learn something from users, and suddenly the thing you were optimizing is less important. So I think of it as a strong commitment for a period of time, not forever. You commit hard, you check in regularly, and if the evidence says the target was wrong, you change it quickly rather than defending it out of pride.

r001.rationale: It says startup objectives should be revisable as circumstances change, and that the team should change the target when evidence shows it is wrong.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that at a startup, you mostly don't get to define a group's objective the way you would in academia or in a big lab. In a PhD, your objective is basically whatever you find interesting, and the constraint is your own taste and your advisor's patience. In a big lab, the objective is often handed down, and your job is to find the slice of it where you can make a difference. At a startup, the objective is forced on you by survival. The question isn't "what's the most interesting thing to work on," it's "what's the thing that, if we don't do it in the next six months, the company doesn't exist."

So the first thing I'd say is that a group's objective should be derived backwards from what the company needs to be true, not forwards from what the group is good at. That sounds obvious, but it's really easy to violate. Everyone comes in with their skills, their favorite problems, the things they did their thesis on, and the natural instinct is to form a team around those capabilities. But then you end up with a very nice research direction that doesn't actually move anything the company cares about.

The second thing is that the objective has to be measurable in a way that connects to the product, even if the group is doing something that looks like research. When I was working on agents, like with ReAct or the later work on language agents, the thing that made it productive was always having a concrete environment where you could tell whether the agent got better. At a startup, the environment is the product itself. If you can't say "this group's work shows up as this number going up for users," then the group's objective is probably too abstract, and you should keep decomposing until you can.

The third thing, and this is more of a cultural point, is that a group's objective should be small enough that one person can hold the whole thing in their head and feel personally responsible for it. Startups are fast because there's very little coordination overhead, and the moment you define an objective that requires four teams to agree on an interface before anyone can make progress, you've lost that advantage. I'd rather have a group with a slightly narrower goal that it fully owns, and then expand the goal once they've proven something works.

And finally, I think you have to be willing to redefine the objective often, maybe every few weeks. In research, people feel bad about changing direction because it looks like the previous work was wasted. At a startup, changing direction is the default, because you're learning what the world actually wants faster than you can plan for it. So the objective is less a destination and more a current best guess, and the group's real job is to update that guess as quickly as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says a startup group should be willing to redefine its objective often, perhaps every few weeks, as it learns.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: why does this group need to exist? At a startup, you have very limited time and people, so the objective should connect directly to something the company needs to figure out or deliver.

I would distinguish the objective from the approach. “Build an agent” is an approach. “Help users finish this particular task reliably” is closer to an objective. Once you phrase it that way, you can ask: what would count as success? What is the biggest uncertainty? What can we do in the next few weeks to learn whether this is working?

You also need a shared understanding of the tradeoffs. If one person is optimizing for research novelty and another is optimizing for shipping next week, both can be doing good work individually while the group makes very little progress. So defining the objective is partly about making those choices explicit.

And I think it should be revisable. You want enough stability that people can focus, but you’re a startup—you’re still learning what matters. The goal is to give people a clear reason for their work and a way to tell whether they’re making progress.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the objective should be revisable because a startup is still learning what matters, clearly conveying that objectives may change over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what uncertainty is this group supposed to resolve? At a startup, you often don’t know exactly what the product should be or which approach will work. So an objective shouldn’t just be a list of things to build. It should explain what you want to achieve and what evidence would tell you that you’re making progress.

You also have to connect that to the company’s current bottleneck. If the biggest uncertainty is whether users want something, making the system more efficient may not be the most valuable objective yet. A group can execute very well locally and still contribute very little to the company.

So I would make the objective clear, give the group room to choose how to pursue it, and revisit it as you learn. You want enough stability for people to focus, but enough flexibility to change direction when the underlying assumptions turn out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says to revisit the objective as the group learns and leave room to change direction when assumptions prove wrong, clearly indicating objectives may change over time.
